meta.location: The land northward, the land southward, and the narrow neck
meta.date: From Shez after the dearth down to Com
meta.unit: The kings from Shez to Com (Ether 10)
principles: A people rebuilt from one household
A prison run as a workshop
A justice that stops short of the man giving it

world_behind.title: One household survived the famine
world_behind.text: Verse 1 says Heth and all his house perished except Shez.

world_behind.title: Riplakish reigned forty and two years
world_behind.text: Verse 8 gives Riplakish forty and two years before the rebellion. The book dates only six reigns at all, at Ether 9:25, 10:8, 10:13, 10:15, 10:30 and 10:32; the other twenty-odd kings in the line are placed by succession alone, which is why this chapter reads as a list rather than a chronology.

world_behind.title: Morianton took the throne with outcasts
world_behind.text: Verse 9 says he gathered an army of them.

world_behind.title: Levi served forty and two years in captivity
world_behind.text: Verse 15 gives the term before he took the kingdom.

world_behind.title: The serpents ended under Lib
world_behind.text: Verse 19 has the poisonous serpents destroyed in the days of Lib. Ether 9:31 to 33 had them hedge up the way southward during the famine two chapters earlier, so a barrier that stood for several reigns comes down in one clause.

world_behind.title: The land southward was kept as a game reserve
world_behind.text: Verse 21 says they preserved the land southward for a wilderness, to get game. Alma 22:31 describes the same country from the Nephite side as a wilderness filled with wild animals, part of which had come from the land northward for food. Two records describe one hunting ground.

world_behind.title: Four generations were born and died in captivity
world_behind.text: Verse 31 names Heth, Aaron, Amnigaddah, and Coriantum.

words.text: Payments a ruler requires. The record uses the word six times, twice in this chapter, and the King James Bible once. Verse 5 attaches them to a building program.
Purified by heat. It appears twice in the record and five times in the King James Bible. Verse 7 has the work done inside a prison.
People put out of a community. It appears twice in the record, and the King James Bible seven times. Verse 9 makes them an army.
Trade carried on between people. Treated at 4 Nephi 1:46. It appears three times in the record and never in the King James Bible.
A soft red metal. The record uses the word eight times and the King James Bible once. Verse 23 lists it with gold, silver, and iron.
To beat grain loose from the stalk. The record uses the word once, here, and never the King James Bible in this spelling.
Made with unusual care and skill. Treated at 1 Nephi 16:10. The word turns up six times here, and the King James Bible ten, usually of woven work.

phrases.term: Shez began to build up again a broken people
phrases.text: The chapter's opening job. What he starts with is one surviving household.

phrases.term: He did remember the destruction of his fathers
phrases.text: Moroni's reason for the righteous kingdom. Memory is given as the cause.

phrases.term: Did lay that upon men's shoulders which was grievous to be borne
phrases.text: The description of the tax. Matthew 23:4 uses nearly the same words of a different burden.

phrases.term: His fine gold he did cause to be refined in prison
phrases.text: Where the king's finest work came from. Verse 6 has already said who was in there.

phrases.term: Gathered together an army of outcasts
phrases.text: The material Morianton built with. Verse 10 has him ease the burden once he holds the throne.

phrases.term: He did do justice unto the people, but not unto himself
phrases.text: Moroni's whole verdict on Morianton, in one clause. The verse names the cause in the next breath.

phrases.term: In the days of Lib the poisonous serpents were destroyed
phrases.text: The end of the blockade set up at Ether 9:33. The land southward opens in the same verse.

phrases.term: A great city by the narrow neck of land
phrases.text: The city placed at the crossing point. Alma 22:32 describes the same kind of neck from the Nephite side.

phrases.term: They did cast up mighty heaps of earth to get ore
phrases.text: Mining described by the spoil it leaves. Four metals are named in the same verse.

phrases.term: Never could be a people more blessed than were they
phrases.text: Moroni's summary of the whole prosperity list. Verse 28 credits it to the hand of the Lord.

phrases.term: They adopted the old plans, and administered oaths after the manner of the ancients
phrases.text: The same oaths returning under Com. Ether 8:15 gave their origin.

verses.label: v. 3
verses.title: A rebellion ended by an unrelated crime
verses.text: The record disposes of a civil war in half a sentence: the son rebels, and then "Shez was smitten by the hand of a robber, because of his exceeding riches, which brought peace again unto his father." The rebel is not defeated in battle or reconciled; he is killed for his money by someone the narrative never mentions again. The record supplies a motive for the robber and none for the peace, and the whole episode takes one verse in a chapter that will spend six on manufacturing.

verses.label: v. 5–7
verses.title: A tyranny described entirely through its finances
verses.text: The record does not call the king proud or cruel in the abstract. It lists policies: heavy taxes, spacious buildings paid for out of them, "an exceedingly beautiful throne," prisons for those who refused to pay and for those who could not, compulsory labor for the prisoners' own support, and death for refusal to work. Verse 7 then closes the loop, "his fine gold he did cause to be refined in prison." The phrase describing the burden, "which was grievous to be borne," matches Matthew 23:4, where the same words describe burdens laid on men's shoulders.

verses.label: v. 10–11
verses.title: A ruler given opposite verdicts at once
verses.text: The record splits the judgment along a line between office and person: "he did do justice unto the people, but not unto himself because of his many whoredoms; wherefore he was cut off from the presence of the Lord." Verse 10 has already recorded the popular verdict, that easing the burden gained him favor and the people "did anoint him to be their king." Public competence and private conduct are assessed separately and the second one settles his standing, which is the reverse of how the chapter treats Riplakish, condemned for what he did to the people.

verses.label: v. 19–21
verses.title: A land management policy stated as such
verses.text: The record reports a deliberate arrangement rather than a drift of settlement: "they did preserve the land southward for a wilderness, to get game," while "the whole face of the land northward was covered with inhabitants." Verse 20 fixes a city to a landmark, "by the narrow neck of land, by the place where the sea divides the land." Verse 19 supplies the occasion, the destruction of the poisonous serpents that had blocked the way south at Ether 9:31–33, so a plague reported two chapters earlier is what makes this policy possible.

verses.label: v. 22–28
verses.title: Six verses of manufacture, then a superlative
verses.text: The record inventories production at length: metals worked and dug, "mighty heaps of earth to get ore," silks and fine-twined linen, tools to plow, sow, reap, hoe, and thrash, tools for working beasts, weapons of war, and "all manner of work of exceedingly curious workmanship." Trade is named too, "they did buy and sell and traffic one with another, that they might get gain." Verse 28 then delivers the verdict on all of it, "never could be a people more blessed than were they." The same catalogue of riches is an indictment at Alma 4:6 and a blessing here, with the difference located in the disposition rather than in the goods.

verses.label: v. 30–31
verses.title: One formula repeated for five generations
verses.text: The record reports a dynasty that never leaves prison: Hearthom loses the kingdom and serves "all the remainder of his days," then Heth "lived in captivity all his days," Aaron "dwelt in captivity all his days," Amnigaddah "also dwelt in captivity all his days," and Coriantum "dwelt in captivity all his days." Four uses of one clause inside verse 31. No war, no ruler, and no reason is named for any of it. Five generations of the royal line are disposed of by a phrase the record simply repeats.

chapter.title: The chapter is a king list with two long pauses
chapter.text: Verses 5 through 8 stop for Riplakish and verses 22 through 28 stop for the workmanship.

chapter.title: A tax is described by what it built
chapter.text: Verse 5 runs the money straight into spacious buildings and a beautiful throne.

chapter.title: The prisons were also workshops
chapter.text: Verse 7 has the king's finest gold refined by the men verse 6 put inside.

chapter.title: A rebel becomes a good administrator
chapter.text: Verse 9 has Morianton take the land by force and verse 10 has him ease the burden.

chapter.title: Justice stops at the man giving it
chapter.text: Verse 11 grants Morianton the people's case and denies him his own.

chapter.title: Four generations pass their whole lives in captivity
chapter.text: Verse 31 names them one after another with the same clause each time.

chapter.title: The prosperity list is mostly tools
chapter.text: Verses 25 through 27 give plow, sow, reap, hoe, thrash, harness, and weapons.

chapter.title: The oaths come back at the close
chapter.text: Verse 33 has robbers pick up the old plans, and verse 34 says Com could not prevail.

applications.title: Build again on what is left
applications.text: Shez began with one surviving household and a broken people.

applications.title: Remember what the generation before you went through
applications.text: Moroni credits Shez's righteous kingdom to that memory.

applications.title: Who made the beautiful thing
applications.text: Riplakish's fine gold was refined in prison, and all his fine workmanship was wrought there. Beautiful output says nothing about the conditions that made it unless somebody records who did the making.

applications.title: Easing the burden is what bought the crown
applications.text: Morianton took the kingdom by force, then eased the people's burden, and they anointed him king. Power seized can be made legitimate by what is done with it, and the record keeps both halves without letting either excuse the other.

applications.title: Check whether your justice reaches you
applications.text: Morianton dealt fairly with the people and not with himself.

applications.title: Leave some ground unbuilt
applications.text: They preserved the land southward as a wilderness to get game while the north filled with inhabitants. A deliberate decision not to develop something is a form of provision, and it has to be made while there is still open ground.

applications.title: Four generations lived their whole lives inside it
applications.text: Hearthom, Heth, Aaron, Amnigaddah and Coriantum each dwelt in captivity all their days. The record spends five names on people who never got out, which is an honest picture of how long some situations run.

applications.title: Keep at it while you are losing
applications.text: Com fought the robbers without prevailing, and the record keeps the fighting.

questions.text: What is left that I could build on?
What have my fathers been through that I ought to remember?
What am I laying on other people's shoulders?
Whom have I written off as an outcast?
Where do I hold others to a standard I skip myself?
Have I taken account of how much I have been given?
What am I still fighting that I have not won?
